source: Integrate a(t) once for v(t) and again for x(t), using the starting values to fix the constants.
Students forget the constants of integration, losing the starting velocity or position.

Newton's second law hands us the acceleration, not the position. So the usual job in mechanics runs the other way from Acceleration as a Derivative: start from $a(t)$ and work back to $v(t)$ and $x(t)$. That is antidifferentiation, and as in Antiderivatives with Initial Conditions, each step brings a constant that the starting conditions decide.

$$\role{velocity}{v}(t) = \role[initial velocity]{velocity}{v_0} + \int_0^t \role{acceleration}{a}(t')\,dt', \qquad \role{position}{x}(t) = \role[starting position]{position}{x_0} + \int_0^t \role{velocity}{v}(t')\,dt'.$$ The area under the $a$–$t$ graph from 0 to $t$ is the change in velocity; the area under the $v$–$t$ graph is the change in position.

The fundamental theorem of calculus says $\int_0^t \dfrac{dv}{dt'}\,dt' = v(t) - v(0)$. Since $dv/dt = a$, the integral of the acceleration is the change in velocity, and adding the starting velocity gives the velocity itself. In pictures: each thin strip of the $a$–$t$ graph has area $a\,\Delta t$, the small change in velocity during that sliver of time; adding up the strips gives the total change.
$a(t) = 6 - 2t$. The shaded area from 0 to $t$ is $\Delta v = 6t - t^2$ (in m/s). After 3 s the area starts to subtract.
A cart has $a(t) = 6t - 4$ (m/s², s). At $t = 0$ its velocity is $2\ \text{m/s}$. Find $v(t)$ and $v(2)$.
The same cart starts at $x_0 = -1\ \text{m}$. Where is it at $t = 2\ \text{s}$?

Dropping the constants of integration. If you write $v(t) = 3t^2 - 4t$ for the cart, you have silently assumed it started from rest; the 2 m/s it already had disappears, and every later velocity and position is off. Check: substitute $t = 0$ into your $v(t)$ and $x(t)$. You must get back the starting velocity and position.
A car starts from rest at $x = 0$ with $a(t) = 4e^{-t/2}$ (m/s², s). How fast is it going at $t = 4\ \text{s}$?
As $t \to \infty$ the speed approaches 8 m/s, the total area under the $a$–$t$ curve.
